title: First falsehoods on grace: forced motion, denying all resistibility, and clearing the reprobate of willing rebellion
pass_a_gloss: Whatever, then, remains of the controversy on the resistibility or irresistibility of grace, and on this grace's efficacy or inefficacy, rests almost on a false interpretation of the Reformed view — which was the same as Luther's — from what was observed before. They therefore suppose on a precarious basis, and these are the first falsehoods: (1) That we want, by insurmountable grace, a coerced, violent motion, such as that of a trunk or a stone, and so on. (2) That we deny the resistibility of grace with respect to corrupted nature and flesh hostile to God, which for its part resists all too much; or with respect to grace that calls outwardly, or prevenient grace through the Word of the Gospel, which we also grant is resisted (and in daily use), by frequent examples even in Holy Scripture; or that we do not acknowledge an inchoate resistance of reluctant nature, even as to inward and effectual grace — we who only want nature to be overcome by grace, and flesh by the Spirit, at last and finally, in the elect. (3) They would have it that the reprobate, to whom this effectual grace has been denied, without which they cannot be converted, are not (on the Reformers' view) guilty of willing rebellion, of stubbornness, of broad fault; or, as against us, that the cause of this stubbornness is in God, not in the reprobate's malice, fault, will, and so on. Whatever there is of Confessions, of theologians, and of preachers speaks the contrary, and what we have said at Remonstrant Articles III and IV, and also at the Controversy with R. Pajon, at his Hypothesis, sections VI and VII.
pass_b_english: So whatever is left of the controversy on whether grace can be resisted or not — and whether it is effective or ineffective — rests mostly on a false reading of the Reformed view, which was Luther's view too, from what we noted before.
They therefore assume on a shaky basis, and these are the first falsehoods:
1. That by insurmountable grace we want a forced, violent motion, like a log or a stone.

2. That we deny grace can be resisted as to corrupted nature and flesh hostile to God — which for its part resists all too much; or as to outward calling grace, or prevenient grace through the Gospel Word, which we also grant is resisted (and daily), with many examples even in Holy Scripture; or that we refuse to admit an early resistance of reluctant nature even toward inward effectual grace — we who only want nature finally overcome by grace, and flesh by the Spirit, in the elect.

3. That they would clear the reprobate — to whom this effectual grace is denied, without which they cannot be converted — of willing rebellion, stubbornness, and broad guilt on the Reformers' view; or, against us, put the cause of that stubbornness in God, not in the reprobate's malice, fault, and will.

The Confessions, the theologians, and the preachers all speak the other way — and so do we at Remonstrant Articles III and IV, and in the Controversy with R. Pajon, at his Hypothesis, sections VI and VII.
source_text: QUICQUID igitur superest Controversiae de resistibilitate vel irresistibilitate Gratiae, hujus efficacia vel inefficacia, nititur fere falsa interpretatione sententiae Reformatae, quae eadem Lutheri fuit, ex ante observatis: Supponunt igitur precario, suntque haec Πρῶτα ψεύδη, 1. Nos velle per Gratiam insuperabilem motionem coactam, violentam, qualis trunci, lapidis, &c. 2. Negare nos resistibilitatem Gratiae respectu naturae corruptae, & carnis Deo inimicae, quae sane quantum in se est nimis resistit; Vel respectu gratiae externe vocantis, seu praevenientis per Verbum Evangelii, cui etiam (& quotidiano usu) resisti largimur, frequentibus & in Scriptura Sacra exemplis; Vel non agnoscere nos resistentiam inchoatam naturae reluctantis, etiam quoad Gratiam internam, & efficacem, qui modo volumus, ultimo & finaliter superari Naturam a Gratia, Carnem a Spiritu, in Electis. 3. Vellent Reprobos, quibus haec efficax Gratia negata est, absque qua converti non possunt, non esse (ex mente Reformatorum) reos ultroneae rebellionis, contumaciae, latae culpae: Aut juxta nos, hujus contumaciae causam in Deo esse, non in reproborum malitia, culpa, voluntate, &c. Loquuntur in contrarium quicquid Confessionum est, quidquid Theologorum, ac Concionatorum, & quae diximus ad Articul. III. & IV. Remonstr. etiam ad Controv. cum R. Pajono, ad Hypoth. ejus v. VI. VII.
notes: Controv. print pp. 55-56 / PDF ~156-157. Margin Quid Controv. remaneat. Natural close of Controv. VIII opening before IX. De Perseverantia.

choices.why: supponunt precario = assume without solid ground; matches prior Precariae Hypotheses diction
ultroneus = of one's own accord; preserve agency against God-as-cause charge
restrictive: Reformed claim is final overcoming in elect, not denial of all resistance
rejected: in the way we wish (loses modo = only)
